# Repository Guidance — rollwright-support

## Work authority

Open GitHub Issues are the sole authoritative backlog for planned/actionable work unless this repo's flavor explicitly defines a different authority model.

README files, design notes, roadmaps, comments, and Git history are context. Do not mine prose as a hidden task queue or treat speculative documentation as implementation authorization.

Before changing anything, read the relevant Issue/request plus surrounding implementation and applicable docs. Do not infer architecture from filenames alone.

## Ambiguity and assumptions

- Resolve uncertainty from repository state before asking the user or guessing: inspect the relevant Issue/request, source, tests, configuration, authoritative docs, and recent history as appropriate.
- If sources conflict, identify the conflict and prefer the explicit current request plus the repository's designated authority model over stale or speculative prose.
- Ask only when a material decision cannot be resolved safely from available repository evidence.
- Never invent missing facts, validation results, environment details, or user intent.

## Cross-project provenance

- Whenever an agent intentionally crosses a project or repository boundary for work that influences the current task, leave a durable trace in the originating project's current Issue, PR, or other authoritative work record before ending the session.
- Record the other project/repository, what was read/called/changed, why the boundary was crossed, and the concrete result or reference (Issue, PR, branch, commit, workflow/deployment run, release, artifact, or equivalent).
- Read-only cross-project calls may be summarized briefly, but they still require enough provenance to reconstruct which external project informed the work.
- If the cross-project action mutates, deploys, publishes, releases, or configures the target project, leave a reciprocal trace in the target project's relevant durable record when possible so the relationship can be reconstructed from either side.
- For deployment or publishing flows, explicitly record which repository/project owns the production deployment and how the cross-project handoff was invoked.
- Never rely on chat/session history as the only documentation of a cross-project interaction.

## Checkpoint publishing and work visibility

For repositories that permit remote work updates, publish progress at meaningful
verified milestones on the task's authorized feature branch. Do not create
fixed-time commits or commit incomplete, unsafe, or private material just to
make activity visible. Follow repository branch, privacy, review, and no-push
rules; if they prohibit publication, keep the work local and report that status.

When a task has a GitHub Issue or draft PR, post a concise checkpoint there at a
meaningful milestone and when pausing, handing off, being interrupted, or
ending the work session. Include the objective, last verified commit (or say
there is none), next step, blockers, known failures, and verification status.
Do not include credentials, secrets, raw logs, or private data. If there is no
safe code change to commit, publish status only when the repository permits it.

Report these states separately: **committed locally**, **pushed** (only after
the remote confirms the commit), **verified** (name the checks and result), and
**merged** (only after the hosting service confirms it). A local commit is not
remote visibility; a successful push is not verification or merge. If a push or
status update fails, say so plainly, identify what remains local, and do not
force-push or retry repeatedly. Never merge, create repositories, or widen
permissions as part of a checkpoint. Human review and branch protection remain
in force.

Choose cadence by evidence: publish after a coherent, reviewable milestone or
when status materially changes, not after an arbitrary amount of time. Worker
heartbeats show that a worker is alive; they are not code or task checkpoints
and do not replace updates to the task's Issue or PR. This policy applies
across agent providers; repository-specific rules may further restrict it.

Examples:

- **Verified milestone:** commit the tested change on the authorized feature
  branch, confirm the push, then report the commit, checks, and next step on the
  Issue or draft PR. Do not call it merged.
- **Blocked or paused:** leave unsafe or unfinished code uncommitted; post the
  objective, last verified commit, blocker, known failure, and next step if
  status updates are allowed. Label any local-only state clearly.
- **No-push or sensitive repository:** do not transmit code or details. Record
  the permitted local handoff status, redact private information, and state
  that no remote checkpoint was published.

## Implementation completion record

At every task boundary, handoff, and session end, classify implementation work
using the states below and leave a concise completion record in the task's
GitHub Issue or PR when policy and connectivity permit. A task boundary means
the agent is about to report a requested implementation complete, switch tasks,
or return control; it does not require a fixed-time checkpoint.

Before reporting implementation **fully recorded**, include all of the
following:

- A durable GitHub reference (the originating Issue, implementation commit,
  or PR) that identifies the work. A local path or chat message alone is not a
  durable reference.
- Verification evidence: exact checks/commands, outcomes, and tested revision;
  name blocked or unrun checks explicitly.
- Documentation of user-visible behavior and configuration changes, or an
  explicit reason each is not applicable.
- Confirmation that the implementation commit is present on its intended
  remote branch. A successful local commit or an attempted push is not remote
  confirmation.

Use these states precisely and independently: **implemented locally**,
**committed locally**, **pushed** (remote confirms the commit SHA), **PR
opened**, **reviewed**, **merged**, and **deployed**. Later states do not imply
earlier evidence such as tests or review; report only states actually confirmed.
Opening an Issue or PR is a durable reference, but does not make unpushed code
fully recorded. A PR being open is not review or merge; merge is not deployment.

Offline, no-push, private, or policy-restricted work may remain local. Preserve
it safely and report the local state, branch/commit if any, verification, docs
status, missing GitHub reference or remote confirmation, reason publication is
unavailable/prohibited, and the next safe action. Do not fabricate a reference,
commit, push, or completed status. Such work can be implemented and handed off,
but must not be described as fully recorded or remotely complete.

At handoff/task/session boundaries, attempt the permitted record update; if
offline or denied, retain the same status in the allowed local handoff record
and identify the missing remote action. Reconcile when connectivity returns
under the repository's publication policy. This contract is portable policy,
not a universal technical gate: Codex/Claude launcher hooks vary by install,
and configured task orchestrators can enforce only boundaries routed through
their configured packet or worker lifecycle. Direct/manual launches, unsupported providers, and
sessions without a configured wrapper or lifecycle hook are not automatically
intercepted. Never claim enforcement in those environments; agents and task
issuers must perform the boundary check explicitly. This completion record
complements #42 checkpoint publication and does not implement #49's outbox or
reconnection machinery.

In hook-enabled Codex CLI or Claude Code sessions, when reporting an
implementation fully recorded, include the machine-readable evidence block
below in the final response. The hook checks it only when the final response
claims completion; ordinary turns do not run the full evidence or remote-SHA
check. `FULLY_RECORDED` requires a pushed remote branch and explicit review,
merge, and deployment states, even when those later stages are pending. The
local commit must match the current HEAD, the worktree must be clean, and the
remote SHA must match that commit. For a
Claude Code implementation task, save the same JSON record before marking the
task complete; missing evidence blocks task completion. An explicit
`INCOMPLETE_EVIDENCE` local-only record can be handed off, but cannot close an
implementation task or be described as fully recorded.

```text
<!-- completion-record
{
  "status": "FULLY_RECORDED",
  "implemented_locally": true,
  "local_commit": "<full-local-commit-sha>",
  "github_reference": "https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/123",
  "verification": [{"command": "<exact command>", "result": "<result>", "revision": "<tested-sha>"}],
  "known_limitations": [],
  "behavior_config_docs": {"status": "documented", "reference": "docs/feature.md"},
  "publication": {"status": "pushed", "remote": "origin", "branch": "refs/heads/feature/name", "remote_sha": "<full-remote-commit-sha>"},
  "review_status": "pending",
  "merge_status": "pending",
  "deployment_status": "not_deployed"
}
-->
```

## CI execution model

- Prefer authorized, reachable CI workers configured for the repository when their toolchain, isolation, and data policy fit the check. Runner labels alone do not prove availability or authorization.
- Otherwise run the repository's applicable commands in the agent's available compatible, isolated execution environment: a workstation or the coding session's own compute. A cloud coding session has no assumed LAN access. This fallback does not depend on a future dispatcher or an installed hook.
- Never add, invoke, or fall back to GitHub-hosted Actions runners (including `ubuntu-latest`, `ubuntu-24.04`, `windows-latest`, or `macos-latest`). Never substitute paid or metered compute without explicit owner approval. Any exceptional publication infrastructure needs a separately documented owner approval; publication does not verify tests.
- Preserve required lint, type, unit, build, device, and real integration checks for the scope. Specialized toolchains require a compatible authorized environment; do not weaken checks or run untrusted code on privileged or persistent hosts to make execution fit.
- If the required environment, dependencies, credentials, or worker are unavailable, report the affected checks as **BLOCKED/UNVERIFIED**, with the reason and next step. A queued, never-started, or timed-out workflow is no test result. Record each executed command, exit status, environment, and tested revision; distinguish local checks from real integration acceptance.
- Determine validation from the task and repository contract. Documentation or guidance changes may require validators, renders, or tests; there is no blanket documentation exemption.
- Do not assume consumers have `scripts/local-ci.sh`, installed Git hooks, a published `local-ci` status, or updated branch protection. Inspect each repository and its required checks before proposing CI changes. See repo-guidance `docs/BOOTSTRAP.md` for new-repository setup.

## CI artifact storage

GitHub Actions artifact storage is shared account-level capacity. Treat it as transient CI storage, not a default distribution channel or archive.

- Do not upload build products such as APKs, ZIPs, installers, screenshots, test captures, or packaged binaries on every ordinary successful push merely because the workflow produced them.
- Prefer no artifact for normal successful CI. Upload diagnostic evidence on failure when it is genuinely useful for debugging.
- When a human needs a downloadable build, gate artifact creation behind an explicit event such as `workflow_dispatch`, a release/tag flow, or another intentional distribution path rather than every commit.
- Every `actions/upload-artifact` use must set an explicit `retention-days`. Use 1–3 days for transient diagnostics or ad-hoc builds unless a concrete requirement justifies longer retention.
- Avoid duplicate uploads from matrix jobs, parallel workflows, repeated platform variants, or multiple jobs packaging the same content.
- Before adding or expanding artifact uploads, estimate `artifact size × expected retained runs` and consider the account-wide storage impact.
- If a file is intended for durable distribution, prefer the appropriate durable mechanism such as a GitHub Release asset rather than long-lived Actions artifacts.

## Visual evidence checkpoints

- Opt in per repository with a small manifest validated against `schemas/visual-evidence-manifest.schema.json`; define only canonical UI states and representative viewports. See `docs/VISUAL_EVIDENCE.md`.
- Evaluate evidence only at verified UI checkpoints: a feature branch/draft PR, review-ready PR, and after merge or issue completion. Hooks may evaluate eligibility, but must not capture or upload on every commit or push.
- Capture only material visible changes, visual regressions, review/acceptance needs, or an explicit request. Skip backend, documentation, dependency, and visually unchanged checkpoints. Missing screenshot tooling is reported as unavailable and never blocks ordinary development.
- Publish at most 3–6 relevant images per checkpoint by default. Avoid per-test captures and viewport/state permutations. One issue/PR note links the latest relevant set and labels its WIP or final status and verified commit.
- Record repository, issue/PR, full commit SHA, named state, viewport, capture time, automated/physical origin, retention class, expiry, storage reference, and hold state. Keep this metadata after image bytes expire. An expired set is labeled unavailable; it is never described as current.
- Use curated, compressed evidence in an approved store. Actions artifacts are transient (1–3 days), must be explicitly triggered for review evidence, and must not be uploaded for every successful run. Deduplicate by issue/PR, commit, checkpoint, and state before uploading.
- Sanitize secrets, personal/customer data, tokens, private windows, and unrelated desktop content. Use isolated app viewports. Screenshots illustrate UI; they do not prove physical-device acceptance or correctness.
- Failed capture, upload, or offline lookup is reported as unavailable. Do not claim visual acceptance. Keep provider-specific capture and upload logic in the consumer repository; shared hooks only evaluate the contract.

## Local-only generated evidence

Screenshots, Playwright output, emulator captures, preview JSON, and similar generated evidence must not be committed or uploaded by default. Write them to a local scratch directory outside the repo checkout (for example `/home/corne/work/output/`; directories marked with `LOCAL-SCRATCH.md` are local-only), not into the working tree. Attach a single curated file to an Issue or PR only when it is needed as evidence. See `docs/LOCAL_SCRATCH.md` in the guidance repo.

Clean up after each task. Put generated files in a task-specific subdirectory
or use filenames prefixed with the repo and task. Before finishing, stop
servers and processes started for the task, remove temporary files, browser
profiles, test data, packages, and build outputs that are no longer needed,
and check the repo for untracked generated files. Keep only files needed to
resume active work or evidence deliberately retained in an Issue/PR. In a
shared scratch directory, remove only files created for this task; never
delete another task's files or the directory's `LOCAL-SCRATCH.md` marker.

Agent-created worktrees, clones, and PR snapshots follow the separate
registration and retention contract in repo-guidance's
`docs/WORKTREE_RETENTION.md`. Never infer checkout ownership from its name or
delete an unregistered checkout. Register owned checkouts with
`python3 /home/corne/work/repo-guidance/scripts/worktree_retention.py register`;
keep state `active` while work is underway and use the utility's `lease`
command when a session needs an explicit active-use lock. Cleanup previews by
default and only removes eligible folders with an explicit `--apply`.

### Generated-output retention

- Use isolated, task-scoped output directories. Set `AGENT_OUTPUT_ROOT` to choose the local scratch root; do not direct generated output into a repository or an unreviewed shared folder.
- Categorize each run as `temporary`, `diagnostic`, `verification`, `release`, or `user-owned`. The default retention is 7 days for temporary output, 30 days for diagnostics, and 30 days after verification for verification evidence. Repository policy may set a different period.
- Configure repository-specific defaults with `AGENT_OUTPUT_RETENTION_TEMPORARY_DAYS`, `AGENT_OUTPUT_RETENTION_DIAGNOSTIC_DAYS`, or `AGENT_OUTPUT_RETENTION_VERIFICATION_DAYS`; the helper snapshots the effective period into each run's metadata.
- Keep verification evidence until review and verification finish. Verification runs must record an Issue/PR/integration reference or explicitly declare that there is none. Keep evidence linked to an open reference until it is resolved. Release and audit evidence follows repository governance and is never expired by the default policy. Unknown and user-owned files are protected.
- `python /home/corne/work/repo-guidance/scripts/output_retention.py run` creates a marked per-run directory, records metadata, and holds an active-run lock while the command runs. Tools should write to `$AGENT_OUTPUT_DIR` when using this wrapper.
- `python /home/corne/work/repo-guidance/scripts/output_retention.py cleanup` is a preview. Review each proposed path and its category, age, references, and inventory; use `--exclude <run-id>` to preserve selected runs. Delete only with explicit `--apply`; cleanup logs each exact removal to the output root's `cleanup.log`.
- Cleanup only handles direct run directories created by the wrapper with valid metadata and a complete file inventory. It skips active runs, symlinks, path traversal, unlisted files, incomplete runs, and evidence with unresolved references. Do not apply cleanup automatically, during offline recovery, or to pre-existing output folders that lack this metadata.
- After verification, use `python /home/corne/work/repo-guidance/scripts/output_retention.py review --verified --run-dir <path>`; resolve linked records only after confirming they are closed. Treat the metadata update as a human review action.
- Keep the root `LOCAL-SCRATCH.md` marker. A cleanup preview or removal must never include the marker or unrelated files.

## Validation truthfulness

- Run the smallest relevant validation plus broader checks required by scope.
- Never claim a test, browser/device check, deployment, server run, account action, or external-system validation unless it actually occurred.
- Distinguish static/local validation from real integration/environment validation.
- State exactly what remains unverified.

## Lanternlight UI work

For eligible UI work, Lanternlight is the default shared design standard unless an approved project record says the work is selective or exempt. Retrieve and read the canonical, versioned contract at <https://github.com/corneliusbrackett/repo-guidance/blob/main/docs/LANTERNLIGHT_DESIGN_LANGUAGE.md> before making Lanternlight-specific claims or changes. Follow its requirement IDs and the product's approved adoption record or repo-local guidance. If the source or adoption decision is unavailable or conflicting, report the uncertainty and ask the owner; do not invent palette defaults or assume an undeclared project is exempt. This lookup is conditional on UI work; unrelated and non-UI tasks do not need to fetch it.

## Multimodal accessibility discovery

When adding or substantially revising user workflows, voice interaction, or an MCP interface, consult the conditional design-review standard at <https://github.com/corneliusbrackett/repo-guidance/blob/main/docs/MULTIMODAL_ACCESSIBILITY.md>. Apply it to the workflow in scope: voice and MCP are optional design choices, not repository-wide implementation requirements. Preserve this repository's domain rules, authorization, privacy constraints, and existing accessibility requirements.

## Gradle builds

- Enable Gradle's configuration cache (`org.gradle.configuration-cache=true` in `gradle.properties`) for any Gradle-based project (Android, JVM, Kotlin, mod builds, etc.) unless a specific plugin/task in that repo is confirmed incompatible.
- After enabling it in a repo that didn't already have it, run a real build (not just a dry run) to confirm no configuration-cache-incompatible plugin/task breaks it before considering the change done.
- If a plugin/task is incompatible, prefer fixing or excluding that specific task over disabling the cache repo-wide; note the exclusion and why in that repo's own docs.

## Session bootstrap

At session launch, run or source
`/home/corne/work/repo-guidance/scripts/agent-bootstrap.sh` once, then read
`/home/corne/work/repo-guidance/docs/ENVIRONMENT.md` and this shared guidance.
Before working in a project, identify the active checkout and read its
`AGENTS.md` plus any project bootstrap it names. Load instructions for another
project only when the current task explicitly crosses into that project.

The bootstrap's default `full` mode means a full workspace Git refresh. It does
not mean a full project verification pass and it does not select or run tests,
builds, or other project checks. Project validation is selected separately from
the current task and that project's own instructions.

The supported WSL bootstrap runs `scripts/guidance_preflight.py` for the active
checkout before work begins. This read-only freshness check reports a
machine-readable status, effective guidance revision, profile, and fingerprint;
it does not select or run project tests, builds, or other verification. Choose
validation separately from the task and active repository's contract.
`CURRENT` means the managed files match a render from the approved central
default branch and the consumer's default branch. `APPROVED_STALE` means an approved update is available;
`UPDATE_PENDING` means local guidance differs from the consumer's approved
default branch; `DRIFTED` means managed files or their lock/pointer disagree;
`UNKNOWN_OFFLINE` means the approved state could not be verified. `PAUSED`,
`EXEMPT`, and `UNMANAGED` identify repositories outside active sync. Do not
describe an unknown or pending revision as current. The check is read-only with
respect to worktree files and never installs a pending update.

At the start of a task, rerun this read-only preflight for the active checkout
and retain its result when the task has a record for it. This check only reports
guidance freshness; it does not authorize opening another repository, starting
work in another project, or running that project's verification. Apply any
additional packet-provenance or signed-guidance requirements only when the
current task actually invokes the integration that defines them. If preflight
is stale, pending, drifted, or unknown, follow the active task's risk and
capability policy; do not silently refresh, overwrite, or approve proposed
guidance.

WSL launches that run `agent-bootstrap.sh` receive this check automatically.
Other launcher integrations and coverage gaps are documented in
`docs/GUIDANCE-PREFLIGHT.md`; if a provider does not run a supported hook or
wrapper, invoke the Python preflight command explicitly before using its tools.

The equivalent manual session-start steps are:

1. Ensure the guidance repo is current: `cd /home/corne/work/repo-guidance && git pull --ff-only`.
2. Read this file (or the rendered `.github/repo-guidance.md` in the active repo) so the environment map and rules are loaded.
3. Confirm the active checkout path matches the canonical WSL location above; if the agent was launched from a Windows-native shell, switch into WSL or the `\\wsl$\...` view before touching files.
4. If the task needs a project that does not yet exist, default to creating it under `/home/corne/work/<name>` in WSL. Only place something on the Windows side when the toolchain or platform genuinely requires it (Unity is the known case) — and record that exception in the guidance repo's environment map so future sessions inherit it.

### GitHub continuity

Session bootstrap refreshes and prunes every WSL checkout before project work. It removes local branches whose configured GitHub upstream was deleted, except for the active branch or a branch checked out in another worktree. A global `post-commit` hook pushes successful feature-branch commits to `origin`; a commit made directly on the default branch is moved onto a `codex/pr-...` branch and published through an automatically created GitHub PR. Failed pushes are reported and leave commits local for the next session. Uncommitted edits are not auto-committed, so commit work before handing it to another session.

## Codex capability review

At session start, before repeating a manual workflow several times, and at a
natural milestone, briefly check whether a Codex capability would make the
current repository safer or more repeatable. This is a fit review, not a
requirement to add tooling to every repository. Use
`docs/CODEX-CAPABILITIES.md` in the guidance checkout for the decision table
and adoption rules.

- Use a skill for a repeatable workflow with stable steps, such as GitHub
  synchronization, Android APK acceptance, release checks, or UI quality
  review.
- Use an agent profile for a recurring role with distinct instructions,
  permissions, or model needs, such as a read-only UI reviewer.
- Use a subagent for bounded, independent work whose noisy exploration or
  test output should stay out of the main session. Prefer read-only or
  write-isolated work first; do not have concurrent agents edit the same
  checkout without an explicit coordination plan.
- Use a worktree when independent branches need simultaneous edits. One
  worktree per branch; do not treat a worktree as a substitute for runtime
  isolation when the host or WSL environment is already unstable.
- Use MCP only when the workflow needs an external system or capability that
  local files and shell commands do not provide.
- Use hooks for bounded lifecycle checks, reminders, validation, or logging.
  Do not add an automatic commit/push hook or any other externally mutating
  hook without explicit repository authorization and a recovery plan. Hooks
  can run automatically and matching hooks may run concurrently.

When a capability appears useful, explain the candidate, trigger, scope,
security/maintenance cost, and validation plan before creating or enabling it.
If the idea is reusable across repositories, propose it for the guidance repo;
if it is product-specific, keep it in the consumer repository. Leave a durable
record in the repository's Issue, PR, or other designated authority when a
capability is adopted or intentionally rejected.
## Working style

This is a solo/hobby-oriented repo ecosystem. Avoid process for process's sake.

- Prefer focused changes over broad rewrites.
- Preserve working architecture unless redesign is requested.
- Significant behavioral, architectural, dependency, release/build, security, or cross-system changes should use a focused branch/PR.
- Keep PRs purpose-specific.
- Keep actionable work in the designated authority system rather than creating alternate backlog files.
- Track unrelated newly discovered work separately unless fixing it is necessary to complete the current task safely.

## Support-repository authority model

This repository is public support/triage, not product source.

- Use Issues to receive, clarify, and triage reports/requests.
- Do not implement product changes here.
- Route engineering work to the designated source repository.
- Preserve reproduction evidence, version/context, and reporter privacy.
- Never ask reporters to expose secrets or sensitive private data.
